source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 18 (PDF 17-37, printed 14-34); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 18 (Transition Metals), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 In which blocks of the modern periodic table are the transition metals found?
blocks.explanation: Transition metals are found in the d and f blocks of the modern periodic table (18.1).

book_ref.quote: Transition metals, found in d and f blocks of the modern periodic table

blocks.prompt: 2 Transition metals are characterized by:

options.text: high density, conductivity and colourful compounds

blocks.explanation: Transition metals are characterized by high density, conductivity and the ability to form colourful compounds (18.1).

book_ref.quote: are characterized by their high density, conductivity, and ability to form colourful compounds

blocks.prompt: 3 Which metal is called the backbone of human civilization, with a key role in the industrial revolution?
blocks.explanation: Iron stands as the backbone of human civilization; it was used for durable tools and modern steel (18.1).

book_ref.quote: Iron stands as the backbone of human civilization

blocks.prompt: 4 Copper, silver and gold remain essential today in high-end electronics and dentistry because of their:
blocks.explanation: They remain essential in electronics and dentistry due to their exceptional corrosion resistance and conductivity (18.1).

book_ref.quote: essential today in high-end electronics and dentistry

blocks.prompt: 5 A transition metal is placed in the f-block if its outermost electrons are being filled in:
blocks.explanation: Transition metals are d-block if outermost electrons fill d-orbitals and f-block if they fill f-orbitals (18.1).

book_ref.quote: f-block (if their outermost electrons are being filled in f-orbitals)

blocks.prompt: 6 The first row transition elements, on which this chapter focuses, are also called the:
blocks.explanation: The first row transition elements are the 3d-series (18.1).

book_ref.quote: first row transition elements i.e., 3d-series

blocks.prompt: 7 First row transition elements are d-block elements having:

options.text: partially filled d-orbitals in any of their stable oxidation states

blocks.explanation: They have partially filled d-orbitals in any of their stable oxidation states (18.1).

book_ref.quote: having partially filled d-orbitals in any of their stable oxidation state

blocks.prompt: 8 Transition elements get their name because they:

options.text: are found between two noble gases
show transitions between variable oxidation states
change from solid to gas easily

blocks.explanation: They are called transition elements because they show transitions between variable oxidation states (18.1).

book_ref.quote: They are called transition elements because they show transitions between variable oxidation states.

blocks.prompt: 9 The d-block of the periodic table is composed of groups:
blocks.explanation: The d-block elements are composed of groups 3 to 12 (18.1).

book_ref.quote: d-block elements are composed of groups 3 to 12

blocks.prompt: 10 Which two members of the 3d d-block cannot be classified as transition elements?
blocks.explanation: Although the d-block is groups 3 to 12, zinc and scandium cannot be classified as transition elements (18.1).

book_ref.quote: zinc and scandium cannot be classified as transition elements

blocks.prompt: 11 The electronic configuration of the only ion of zinc, Zn²⁺, is:
blocks.explanation: Zn forms only Zn²⁺, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s⁰, which has a complete 3d subshell (18.1).

book_ref.quote: the electronic configuration of Zn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s⁰

blocks.prompt: 12 The electronic configurations of which two 3d elements do not follow the Aufbau principle?
blocks.explanation: Configurations usually follow the Aufbau principle, except in chromium and copper (18.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Electronic configuration of the transition elements usually follows Aufbau principle

blocks.prompt: 13 The ground-state configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is:
blocks.explanation: Chromium is [Ar] 3d⁵4s¹ because a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell gives extra stability (18.1.1, Table 18.1).

book_ref.quote: These two elements show anomaly due to acquiring stability of half-filled (chromium; 3d⁵)

blocks.prompt: 14 Copper (Z = 29) has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s¹ because:

options.text: a completely filled d-subshell gives stability

blocks.explanation: Copper shows the anomaly to acquire the stability of a completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell (18.1.1).

book_ref.quote: completely filled (copper; 3d¹⁰) d-subshell

blocks.prompt: 15 The stabilizing factor of half-filled and filled d-subshells in Cr and Cu:

options.text: makes the electron cloud more symmetrical and gives better shielding

blocks.explanation: This stabilizing factor makes the electron cloud more symmetrical and provides a better shielding effect (18.1.1).

book_ref.quote: makes the electron cloud of these two elements more symmetrical

blocks.prompt: 16 The electronic configuration of Fe³⁺ (Fe, Z = 26) is:
blocks.explanation: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶4s²; Fe³⁺ loses both 4s electrons and one 3d electron: [Ar] 3d⁵4s⁰ (Table 18.1).

book_ref.quote: The electronic configuration of first row of transition elements in their neutral (M⁰)

blocks.prompt: 17 How many 3d electrons are present in Co³⁺ (Co, Z = 27)?
blocks.explanation: Co is [Ar] 3d⁷4s²; Co³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶4s⁰, so it has 6 d electrons (Table 18.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 18.1 Electronic configurations of first row transition elements

blocks.prompt: 18 Which of these dipositive ions has the configuration [Ar] 3d⁵4s⁰?
blocks.explanation: Mn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵4s⁰; Cr²⁺ is 3d⁴, Co²⁺ is 3d⁷ and Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸ (Table 18.1).

book_ref.quote: dipositive (M²⁺) and tripositive (M³⁺) oxidation states are given in the following Table 18.1

blocks.prompt: 19 Which tripositive ion has the configuration [Ar] 3d⁸4s⁰?
blocks.explanation: Cu³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁸4s⁰; Co³⁺ is 3d⁶, Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ and Ni³⁺ is 3d⁷ (Table 18.1).

book_ref.quote: Aufbau principle, except in chromium and copper

blocks.prompt: 20 The first row of transition elements described in this chapter runs from:
blocks.explanation: The first row of transition elements includes the metals from titanium to copper (18.2).

book_ref.quote: The first row of transition elements includes the metals from titanium to copper.

blocks.prompt: 21 Which first row transition metal is reddish brown, while the others are silvery or grey?
blocks.explanation: Except copper, which is reddish brown, the others occur as silvery or grey lustrous metals (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Except copper, which is reddish brown

blocks.prompt: 22 Across the first row of transition metals, the atomic radius:

options.text: usually decreases, but increases a little at the end

blocks.explanation: The atomic radius usually decreases from left to right; at the end it increases a little (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Their atomic radius usually decreases from left to right

blocks.prompt: 23 The small increase in atomic radius at the end of the 3d row is associated with:

options.text: the stability of copper's completely filled d-subshell

blocks.explanation: This increase may be associated with the stability acquired by copper due to its completely filled d-subshell (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: This increase may be associated to the stability acquired by copper

blocks.prompt: 24 The densities of the 3d metals generally increase from titanium to copper because of:

options.text: regular build-up of nuclear charge and atomic size shrinkage

blocks.explanation: Densities increase due to a regular build-up of nuclear charge and atomic size shrinkage (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: This is due to a regular build-up of nuclear charge and atomic size shrinkage.

blocks.prompt: 25 Transition metals are malleable. This means they can be:
blocks.explanation: Malleable means they can be hammered into thin sheets; ductile means drawn into wires (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: malleable (can be hammered into thin sheets)

blocks.prompt: 26 Most transition metals and their compounds are paramagnetic due to:
blocks.explanation: Most of them and their compounds are paramagnetic due to the presence of unpaired d electrons (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: paramagnetic due to the presence of unpaired d electrons

blocks.prompt: 27 The melting and boiling points of the 3d elements from left to right:

options.text: are high and show a variable trend

blocks.explanation: They have high melting and boiling points showing a variable trend (Figure 18.1) (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: show a variable trend from left to right

blocks.prompt: 28 Transition metals form complexes by:

options.text: accepting lone pairs from ligands into vacant d-orbitals
forming ionic bonds with noble gases

blocks.explanation: They form complexes by accepting lone pairs of electrons from ligands into vacant d-orbitals (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: by accepting lone pairs of electrons from ligands into vacant d-orbitals

blocks.prompt: 29 Transition metals form coloured ions and complexes because of:

options.text: electron transitions from lower to higher energy on absorbing light

blocks.explanation: Coloured ions form due to the transition of electrons from lower to higher energy as a result of absorption of light (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: due to the transition of electrons from lower energy to higher energy level

blocks.prompt: 30 Which pair shows the variable oxidation states of iron given in the chapter?
blocks.explanation: Transition metals lose varying numbers of electrons to form stable ions, e.g. Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: they can lose varying number of electrons to form stable ions

blocks.prompt: 31 In first row transition metals, which electrons are involved in chemical bonding?

options.text: Both 4s electrons and electrons of the partially filled 3d subshell

blocks.explanation: Not only the 4s electrons but also the electrons of the partially filled 3d subshell take part in bonding (18.2.3).

book_ref.quote: not only the electrons in the outermost 4s subshell but also the electrons in the partially filled 3d subshell are involved in chemical bonding

blocks.prompt: 32 When a 3d metal atom loses only its 4s electrons, it usually shows the oxidation state:
blocks.explanation: Losing only the 4s electrons usually gives the common +2 oxidation state (18.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Only the 4s electrons, usually giving the common +2 oxidation state.

blocks.prompt: 33 The higher oxidation states of 3d metals arise by losing:

options.text: the 4s electrons plus a variable number of 3d electrons

blocks.explanation: Higher oxidation states arise from loss of the 4s electrons plus a variable number of 3d electrons (18.2.3).

book_ref.quote: The 4s electrons plus a variable number of 3d electrons

blocks.prompt: 34 Which 3d metal shows the maximum oxidation state of +7?
blocks.explanation: Among the 3d metals, Mn has the maximum oxidation state of +7 (18.2.3, Table 18.2).

book_ref.quote: Among these metals, Mn has the maximum oxidation state of +7.

blocks.prompt: 35 The oxidation state of manganese in the manganate(VII) ion, MnO₄⁻ (O = −2), is:
blocks.explanation: x + 4(−2) = −1, so x = +7, the highest state of Mn in Table 18.2 (18.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Table 18.2 Common oxidation states of 3d elements

blocks.prompt: 36 The oxidation states of transition elements vary from left to right within the d-block in a:
blocks.explanation: The oxidation state varies in a parabolic trend from left to right within the d-block (18.2.3).

book_ref.quote: varies in parabolic trend from left to right within d-block

blocks.prompt: 37 The energy difference between the inner 3d subshell and the outermost 4s subshell is:
blocks.explanation: The energy difference between 3d and 4s is very small, so 3d electrons can also easily be lost (18.2.3).

book_ref.quote: The energy difference between the inner 3d subshell and the outermost 4s subshell is very small.

blocks.prompt: 38 A transition metal ion switching between oxidation states to form an unstable intermediate with a reactant usually acts in:
blocks.explanation: Switching oxidation states (e.g. Fe²⁺ ⇌ Fe³⁺) to form an unstable intermediate usually occurs in homogeneous catalysis (18.2.4).

book_ref.quote: This process usually occurs in homogenous catalysis.

blocks.prompt: 39 In the preparation of acrylic acid from acetylene with nickel salts, nickel switches between:
blocks.explanation: Nickel salts used to prepare acrylic acid from acetylene involve the oxidation states Ni(0) and Ni(II) (18.2.4).

book_ref.quote: nickel salts are used in the preparation of acrylic acid from acetylene

blocks.prompt: 40 In the Haber process for ammonia, the heterogeneous catalyst used is:
blocks.explanation: Solid iron accelerates the reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen to form ammonia in the Haber process (18.2.4).

book_ref.quote: the use of solid iron to accelerate the reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen gases

blocks.prompt: 41 In heterogeneous catalysis on a transition metal surface, after the reaction the products:

options.text: desorb, leaving the catalyst ready for the next cycle
change the metal into a gas

blocks.explanation: After the reaction the products desorb and the catalyst is ready for the next cycle (18.2.4).

book_ref.quote: After the reaction, the products desorb

blocks.prompt: 42 The temporary activated complex on a catalyst surface lowers the activation energy because it:

options.text: holds the reactants in the correct orientation

blocks.explanation: The surface complex holds the reactants in the correct orientation, lowering the activation energy (18.2.4).

book_ref.quote: holds the reactants in the correct orientation

blocks.prompt: 43 By forming and breaking down an intermediate, a transition metal catalyst provides a pathway with:
blocks.explanation: The catalyst is regenerated and provides a reaction pathway with lower activation energy (18.2.4).

book_ref.quote: providing a reaction pathway with lower activation energy

blocks.prompt: 44 Transition elements form complex ions mainly because they have:

options.text: vacant d orbitals energetically accessible to accept electron pairs

blocks.explanation: They have vacant d orbitals that are energetically accessible to accept electron pairs (18.3).

book_ref.quote: Transition elements form complex ions because they have vacant (empty) d orbitals

blocks.prompt: 45 The bond formed when a ligand donates a lone pair into a vacant d orbital of a metal ion is:
blocks.explanation: The vacant d orbitals accept lone pairs from ligands, forming coordinate covalent (dative) bonds (18.3).

book_ref.quote: forming coordinate covalent bonds (or dative bonds)

blocks.prompt: 46 In complex formation, the central transition metal ion acts as a:
blocks.explanation: A transition element acts as a Lewis acid (electron pair acceptor) in complex formation (18.3).

book_ref.quote: A transition element acts as a Lewis acid (electron pair acceptor) in complex formation.

blocks.prompt: 47 A ligand acts as a Lewis base because it:
blocks.explanation: A ligand acts as a Lewis base because it donates an electron pair (18.3).

book_ref.quote: It acts as a Lewis base because it donates an electron pair.

blocks.prompt: 48 The word 'ligand' comes from a Latin word meaning:
blocks.explanation: 'Ligand' originates from the Latin 'ligare', meaning 'to bind' (18.3).

book_ref.quote: The word "ligand" originates from the Latin

blocks.prompt: 49 The most abundant type of ligands are:
blocks.explanation: Negatively charged donors, anionic ligands, are the most abundant type, e.g. Cl⁻, CN⁻, OH⁻, C₂O₄²⁻ (18.3).

book_ref.quote: These are the most abundant type of ligands.

blocks.prompt: 50 As a ligand, the cyanide ion CN⁻ is named:
blocks.explanation: Anionic ligand names usually end in '-o': chloride becomes chloro and cyanide becomes cyano (18.3).

book_ref.quote: Their names usually end at

blocks.prompt: 51 The special ligand names of H₂O, NH₃ and CO are respectively:
blocks.explanation: Neutral ligands keep their names, but H₂O is aqua, NH₃ is ammine and CO is carbonyl (18.3).

book_ref.quote: some have special names like H₂O (aqua), NH₃ (ammine) and CO (carbonyl)

blocks.prompt: 52 Which of the following is a cationic ligand?
blocks.explanation: Cationic ligands are rare, with names often ending in '-ium', e.g. NO⁺ (nitrosonium) (18.3).

book_ref.quote: The positively charged electron pair donating species are called cationic ligands.

blocks.prompt: 53 Which one of the following is a bidentate ligand?
blocks.explanation: Bidentate ligands donate two electron pairs, e.g. 1,2-diaminoethane and ethanedioate; H₂O, NH₃ and CN⁻ are monodentate (18.3).

book_ref.quote: Bidentate ligands can donate two electron pairs to the central metal atom/ion.

blocks.prompt: 54 In 1,2-diaminoethane (en), the donor atoms are:

options.text: one nitrogen and one carbon atom

blocks.explanation: In en (H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂), each of the two N atoms donates a lone pair to the metal (18.3).

book_ref.quote: each of the two nitrogen (N) atoms donate a lone pair to the metal

blocks.prompt: 55 In the ethanedioate ion (C₂O₄²⁻), the electron pairs are donated by:

options.text: two oxygen atoms, one from each carboxyl group

blocks.explanation: In C₂O₄²⁻, two oxygen atoms, one from each carboxyl group, donate electron pairs (18.3).

book_ref.quote: two oxygen (O) atoms, one from each carboxyl group

blocks.prompt: 56 EDTA is called a hexadentate ligand because it:

options.text: attaches to a metal ion through six donor atoms
forms six ionic bonds with water

blocks.explanation: EDTA attaches to a metal ion using six donor atoms (four O and two N), so it is hexadentate (18.3).

book_ref.quote: It is a hexadentate ligand because it can attach to a metal ion using six donor atoms

blocks.prompt: 57 A polydentate ligand is one that forms:

options.text: more than two dative bonds to a single central metal ion

blocks.explanation: Polydentate is the general term for any ligand forming more than two dative bonds to one metal ion (18.3).

book_ref.quote: any ligand that forms more than two dative bonds to a single central metal atom/ion

blocks.prompt: 58 What is the coordination number of the metal ion in [Co(en)₃]³⁺?
blocks.explanation: Each en forms two dative bonds, so 3 × 2 = 6 dative bonds: coordination number 6 (18.3).

book_ref.quote: The coordination number determines the overall structure of the complexes.

blocks.prompt: 59 A coordination sphere (central metal ion with its directly bonded ligands) is usually written:
blocks.explanation: The coordination sphere is usually written inside square brackets [Complex] (18.3).

book_ref.quote: is usually written inside square brackets

blocks.prompt: 60 In [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, the total charge of the six ligands is:
blocks.explanation: Six CN⁻ ligands carry 6 × (−1) = −6; with Fe²⁺ (+2) the sphere charge is −4 (18.3, book correction).

book_ref.quote: the central metal ion Fe²⁺ is bonded to six CN⁻ ligands

blocks.prompt: 61 The charge on the central metal ion in a complex is found as:

options.text: charge on sphere plus total charge of ligands
number of ligands times charge on sphere
charge on sphere minus total charge of ligands
always equal to the coordination number

blocks.explanation: The metal charge is the difference of the charge on the sphere and the total charge of the ligands (18.3).

book_ref.quote: the charge on the metal atom or ion will be the difference of the charge on sphere and total charge of ligands

blocks.prompt: 62 What is the coordination number of iron in [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻, where ethanedioate is bidentate?
blocks.explanation: Three bidentate C₂O₄²⁻ ligands form 3 × 2 = 6 dative bonds, so the coordination number is 6 (18.3).

book_ref.quote: In the ethanedioate ion (C₂O₄²⁻)

blocks.text: 18.4 Predicting Formula and Charge of a Complex Ion

blocks.prompt: 63 In the general formula [M(L)ₓ]±ʸ of a complex ion, x is:

options.text: the number of ligands, determined by the coordination number
the atomic number of the metal

blocks.explanation: x is the number of ligands, determined by the coordination number; ±y is the overall charge (18.4).

book_ref.quote: x is the number of ligand (determined by the coordination number)

blocks.prompt: 64 A Cr³⁺ ion bonds to six neutral water ligands. The formula of the complex ion is:
blocks.explanation: Charge = (+3) + 6 × (0) = +3, so the ion is [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (18.4).

book_ref.quote: The formula and charge of a complex ion are determined by combining the central metal ion

blocks.prompt: 65 A Ni²⁺ ion bonds to four CN⁻ ligands. The overall charge of the complex ion is:

book_ref.quote: Metal charge (+2) + (Number of ligands × Ligand charge). A negative sum.

blocks.prompt: 66 In the neutral complex [Ni(CO)₄], the oxidation state of nickel is:
blocks.explanation: CO is neutral, so (0) + 4 × (0) = 0: Ni is in oxidation state 0 (Table 18.3).

book_ref.quote: Place Metal (Ni) first, then Ligand (CO) with its number as a subscript (4), inside brackets [ ].

blocks.prompt: 67 The oxidation state of cobalt in [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]³⁺ is:
blocks.explanation: NH₃ and H₂O are neutral, so the metal charge equals the overall charge, +3 (18.4).

book_ref.quote: Metal charge (+3) + (Number of ligands × Ligand charge). A positive sum.

blocks.prompt: 68 The oxidation state of copper in [CuCl₄]²⁻ is:

book_ref.quote: Table 18.3. Predicting formula and charge of a complex ion

blocks.prompt: 69 An Ag⁺ ion bonds to two CN⁻ ligands. The complex ion is:

book_ref.quote: ±y is the overall charge of the complex ion

blocks.prompt: 70 In a linear complex such as [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, the angle between the two ligands is:
blocks.explanation: In linear geometry the two ligands are on opposite sides at 180°, e.g. [Ag(NH₃)₂]Cl and K[Ag(CN)₂] (18.5).

book_ref.quote: Typical examples of linear complexes are [Ag(NH₃)₂]Cl and K[Ag(CN)₂].

blocks.prompt: 71 Square planar geometry is characteristic of metal ions with the configuration:
blocks.explanation: Square planar geometry is characteristic of d⁸ ions such as Ni²⁺ and Pt²⁺ (18.5).

book_ref.quote: This geometry is characteristic of d⁸ metal ions

blocks.prompt: 72 In a square planar complex, the bond angle between neighbouring ligands is:
blocks.explanation: The metal and four ligands lie in one plane at the corners of a square with bond angle 90° (18.5).

book_ref.quote: at the corners of a square with bond angle 90°

blocks.prompt: 73 The bond angle in a tetrahedral complex such as [CoCl₄]²⁻ is:
blocks.explanation: In tetrahedral complexes four ligands are at the corners of a tetrahedron with bond angle 109.5° (18.5).

book_ref.quote: four ligands are directed at the corners of a tetrahedron with bond angle of 109.5°

blocks.prompt: 74 The most common geometry of transition metal complexes is:
blocks.explanation: Octahedral, with six ligands along the x, y and z axes, is the most common geometry (18.5).

book_ref.quote: This is the most common geometry for transition metal complexes.

blocks.prompt: 75 Which of the following is an octahedral complex?
blocks.explanation: [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is octahedral; [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is square planar, [CoCl₄]²⁻ tetrahedral and [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ linear (18.5).

book_ref.quote: The common examples are [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ and [Co(en)₃]³⁺.

blocks.prompt: 76 The shape of the [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺ ion is:
blocks.explanation: Pt²⁺ is a d⁸ ion; [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺ is a square planar example (18.5).

book_ref.quote: Examples are: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ and [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺.

blocks.prompt: 77 In an octahedral complex, the two ligands above and below the square plane are at an angle to each other of:
blocks.explanation: Four ligands form a square plane (90°) and the other two are above and below the plane at 180° (18.5).

book_ref.quote: coming along the x, y and z axes

blocks.prompt: 78 In an isolated atom, the five d orbitals are:
blocks.explanation: In an isolated atom all five d orbitals have the same energy (degenerate) (18.6).

book_ref.quote: In an isolated atom, all five d orbitals have the same energy (degenerate)

blocks.prompt: 79 The five d orbitals of a metal ion split into two groups in a complex because the approaching ligands:
blocks.explanation: Approaching ligands create an electric field that splits the five d orbitals into two groups with different energies (18.6).

book_ref.quote: they create an electric field that causes the five d orbitals to split

blocks.prompt: 80 In an octahedral complex such as [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺, the lower-energy set of d orbitals is:
blocks.explanation: In octahedral complexes three orbitals dxy, dxz, dyz are lower and two, dx²−y², dz², are higher (Figure 18.4).

book_ref.quote: the five d orbitals split into two sets

blocks.prompt: 81 In a tetrahedral complex such as [CuCl₄]²⁻, the lower-energy set of d orbitals is:
blocks.explanation: In tetrahedral complexes the splitting is inverted: dxy, dxz, dyz higher and dx²−y², dz² lower (Figure 18.5).

book_ref.quote: the splitting is inverted with three higher-energy orbitals

blocks.prompt: 82 Compared with an octahedral complex, the magnitude of d-orbital splitting in a tetrahedral complex is:
blocks.explanation: The magnitude of splitting in tetrahedral complexes is smaller than in octahedral complexes (Figure 18.5).

book_ref.quote: The magnitude of splitting in tetrahedral complexes is smaller than that in octahedral complexes

blocks.prompt: 83 Which ligand causes the largest d-orbital splitting (ΔE) in the chapter's ligand series?
blocks.explanation: Order from high to low ΔE: CN⁻ > en > NH₃ > H₂O > OH⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻ (18.6).

book_ref.quote: Ligands can be arranged in order of their ability to cause d-orbital splitting

blocks.prompt: 84 Which ligand produces the smallest splitting ΔE in the chapter's series?
blocks.explanation: I⁻ is last in the series CN⁻ > en > NH₃ > H₂O > OH⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻, so it gives the smallest ΔE (18.6).

book_ref.quote: for some other ligands like Cl⁻, I⁻, ΔE is smaller

blocks.prompt: 85 A larger splitting ΔE in a complex means that the light absorbed has:
blocks.explanation: A larger ΔE means light of higher frequency (shorter wavelength) must be absorbed (18.6).

book_ref.quote: A larger ΔE means a higher frequency, (shorter wavelength) of light must be absorbed

blocks.prompt: 86 A complex with a large ΔE absorbs violet or blue light. It appears:
blocks.explanation: Absorbing violet/blue light, the complex reflects yellow light and appears yellow (18.6).

book_ref.quote: Corresponding to that a yellow light is reflected giving the compound a yellow colour.

blocks.prompt: 87 A complex that absorbs low-energy red/orange light appears:
blocks.explanation: Complexes absorbing low-energy red/orange light appear blue or green (complementary colours) (18.6).

book_ref.quote: Some complexes absorb low-energy light (red/orange) and appear blue or green

blocks.prompt: 88 Replacing H₂O ligands by NH₃ ligands around a metal ion generally makes ΔE:
blocks.explanation: NH₃ comes before H₂O in the series, so NH₃ causes larger splitting (18.6).

book_ref.quote: Some ligands like NH₃, CN⁻ cause larger splitting

blocks.prompt: 89 If a compound absorbs all of the white light falling on it, it appears:
blocks.explanation: If the white light is absorbed completely, the complex appears black (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: it may get absorbed completely, and the complex appears black

blocks.prompt: 90 A compound that reflects or transmits the whole of white light appears:
blocks.explanation: A compound that reflects or transmits the whole light appears white (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: The compound may reflect or transmit the whole light, and appears to be white.

blocks.prompt: 91 A complex absorbs yellow light. The colour it shows is:
blocks.explanation: The colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed: absorbing yellow, it appears violet (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: if a complex absorbs yellow light, it appears violet

blocks.prompt: 92 The energy ΔE of a d-d transition is related to the wavelength λ of the light absorbed by:
blocks.explanation: By Planck's equation ΔE = hν = hc/λ (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: according to the Planck's equation, ΔE = hν = hc/λ

blocks.prompt: 93 A complex absorbs light of wavelength 500 nm in a d-d transition. Taking h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, ΔE for one transition is:

book_ref.quote: corresponds to a specific frequency (ν) and wavelength (λ) of visible light

blocks.prompt: 94 Light of wavelength 600 nm is absorbed by a complex. With c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, its frequency ν = c/λ is:

book_ref.quote: (h is Planck's constant and c is speed of light)

blocks.prompt: 95 The colour of a transition metal complex is decided by:

options.text: the light that is absorbed only
the unabsorbed light that is transmitted

blocks.explanation: The unabsorbed light is transmitted and decides the nature of the colour (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: The unabsorbed light is transmitted and it decides the nature of the colour.

blocks.prompt: 96 Substitution of ligands in a complex occurs if:

options.text: the new complex formed is more stable
the new complex is less stable
the metal has no d electrons

blocks.explanation: If the new complex is more stable, substitution of ligands occurs and changes colour, structure and reactivity (18.7).

book_ref.quote: The complexes of copper(II) and cobalt(II) ions can be used to show ligand substitution reactions.

blocks.prompt: 97 When we write Cu²⁺(aq), we actually mean the complex ion:
blocks.explanation: Cu²⁺(aq) refers to [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, which gives the blue colour of copper(II) salt solutions (18.7.1).

book_ref.quote: we actually refer to the complex ion [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺

blocks.prompt: 98 Sodium hydroxide is added to copper(II) sulphate solution. The product is:
blocks.explanation: NaOH gives a light blue precipitate, [Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂](s) (18.7.1).

book_ref.quote: On adding sodium hydroxide to a copper(II) solution, a light blue precipitate is formed.

blocks.prompt: 99 When OH⁻ ions react with [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, the number of water ligands replaced is:
blocks.explanation: Two water ligands are replaced by two hydroxide ions, giving [Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂] (18.7.1).

book_ref.quote: Two water ligands are replaced by two hydroxide ions in this reaction.

blocks.prompt: 100 Concentrated ammonia is added to the light blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide complex. What is observed?

options.text: The precipitate dissolves to give a dark blue solution

blocks.explanation: The light blue precipitate dissolves in concentrated ammonia giving a dark blue solution (18.7.1).

book_ref.quote: the light blue precipitate dissolves resulting in a dark blue solution

blocks.prompt: 101 When ammonia exchanges directly with the water ligands of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, how many water molecules are replaced?
blocks.explanation: Four water molecules are replaced: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4H₂O (18.7.1).

book_ref.quote: by replacing four water molecules

blocks.prompt: 102 Concentrated HCl is added drop by drop to blue [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺. The solution formed is:
blocks.explanation: Chloride ions replace the water ligands, giving a yellow solution of [CuCl₄]²⁻ (18.7.1).

book_ref.quote: A yellow solution is obtained that contains the complex ion [CuCl₄]²⁻

blocks.prompt: 103 The colour of an aqueous solution of cobalt(II) sulphate, due to [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺, is:
blocks.explanation: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ gives a pink colour to aqueous cobalt(II) sulphate (18.7.2).

book_ref.quote: This ion gives a pink colour to the aqueous solution of cobalt(II) sulphate.

blocks.prompt: 104 On adding NaOH solution to aqueous cobalt(II) ions, the precipitate formed is:

options.text: blue, and may turn pink on standing

blocks.explanation: A blue precipitate of cobalt(II) hydroxide forms, which may turn pink on standing (18.7.2).

book_ref.quote: which may turn pink on standing

blocks.prompt: 105 The soluble complex formed when excess ammonia reacts with cobalt(II) hydroxide precipitate is named:
blocks.explanation: Ammonia ligands replace the water and hydroxide ligands forming hexaamminecobalt(II), [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ (18.7.2).

book_ref.quote: forming a soluble ammine complex, hexaamminecobalt(II) ions

blocks.prompt: 106 Concentrated HCl is added drop by drop to pink aqueous cobalt(II) ions. The solution turns:
blocks.explanation: Conc. HCl gives a blue solution of the tetrahedral complex [CoCl₄]²⁻ (18.7.2).

book_ref.quote: results in the formation of a blue solution containing the tetrahedral complex

blocks.prompt: 107 Ligand exchange changes the colour of a complex because it changes:

options.text: the atomic number of the metal
the magnitude of d-orbital splitting and so the absorbed frequency
the mass number of the metal
the number of protons in the ligand

blocks.explanation: Ligand exchange changes the splitting ΔE, so the absorbed frequency and observed colour change (18.7.3).

book_ref.quote: The exchange of ligands in a complex changes the magnitude of splitting for the metal ion.

blocks.prompt: 108 According to Table 18.4, adding concentrated NH₃ to blue [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ gives a complex of colour:
blocks.explanation: Table 18.4: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (blue) + conc. NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ (deep blue) (18.7.3).

book_ref.quote: [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ (Deep Blue)

blocks.prompt: 109 Which change is listed in Table 18.4 for pink [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ on adding concentrated NH₃ solution?
blocks.explanation: Table 18.4: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (pink) + conc. NH₃ → [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ (yellow); with conc. HCl it gives blue [CoCl₄]²⁻ (18.7.3).

book_ref.quote: Table 18.4 Ligand exchange and colour change

blocks.text: 18.8 Stability of Complexes and Stability Constant (Kstab)

blocks.prompt: 110 The concentration of water is not written in a Kstab expression because water:

options.text: does not take part in the reaction
is the solvent and its concentration remains constant

blocks.explanation: [H₂O], being the solvent (constant), is omitted from the Kstab expression (18.8).

book_ref.quote: being solvent (remains constant) is omitted from the Kstab expression

blocks.prompt: 111 For [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O, the Kstab expression is:
blocks.explanation: Kstab = [CuCl₄²⁻] ÷ ([Cu(H₂O)₆²⁺][Cl⁻]⁴), with [H₂O] omitted (18.8).

book_ref.quote: When we add a new ligand, it competes with water to bind with the metal ion.

blocks.prompt: 112 Stability constants are usually given on a log₁₀ scale because:

options.text: it makes very large numbers easier to compare

blocks.explanation: Kstab values are very large; the log₁₀ scale makes them easier to compare (18.8).

book_ref.quote: This makes it easier to compare very large numbers.

blocks.prompt: 113 A complex with a high log₁₀ Kstab value:

options.text: is less stable and easily loses ligands
is more stable and its equilibrium lies far to the right

blocks.explanation: Higher log₁₀ Kstab means a more stable complex; the equilibrium lies far to the right (18.8).

book_ref.quote: Higher the log₁₀ Kstab, more stable will be the complex

blocks.prompt: 114 Using Table 18.5 (log₁₀ Kstab: [CuCl₄]²⁻ 5.6, ammonia complex 13.1, [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ 18.8), the most stable copper(II) complex is:
blocks.explanation: [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ has the highest log₁₀ Kstab (18.8), so it is the most stable (18.8).

book_ref.quote: Table 18.5 Stability constants of some Cu(II) complexes

blocks.prompt: 115 The higher stability of complexes with polydentate ligands than with monodentate ligands is called the:
blocks.explanation: Complexes with polydentate ligands have higher stability constants; this is the chelating effect (18.8).

book_ref.quote: This is called chelating effect of the ligands.

blocks.prompt: 116 From Table 18.5, Kstab of [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ (log 18.8) is how many times Kstab of the ammonia complex (log 13.1)?

book_ref.quote: complexes with polydentate ligands have higher stability constant values

blocks.prompt: 117 Ammonia is added to a solution of [CuCl₄]²⁻. What happens?

options.text: Nothing, as chloride complex is more stable
A white precipitate of CuCl forms
Ammonia displaces chloride and the solution turns blue

blocks.explanation: A ligand with higher Kstab displaces one with lower Kstab; the ammonia complex is far more stable, so the solution turns blue (18.8).

book_ref.quote: adding ammonia to a chloride complex will turn the solution blue

blocks.prompt: 118 For [CuCl₄]²⁻, log₁₀ Kstab = 5.6. At equilibrium with [Cl⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, the ratio [CuCl₄²⁻] ÷ [Cu(H₂O)₆²⁺] is about:

book_ref.quote: Stability constants are usually provided on a log₁₀ scale.

blocks.prompt: 119 Stereoisomers of a complex have the same formula and bonds but differ in:

options.text: the arrangement of ligands in space

blocks.explanation: Stereoisomers have the same formula and bonds but differ in the arrangement of ligands in space (18.9).

book_ref.quote: differ with respect to the arrangement of ligands in space are called stereoisomers

blocks.prompt: 120 In the cis isomer of a square planar or octahedral complex, the identical ligands are:
blocks.explanation: In cis isomers identical ligands are adjacent (90°); in trans they are opposite (180°) (18.9.1).

book_ref.quote: identical ligands are present at either adjacent (90° angle, cis)

blocks.prompt: 121 Which isomer of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is used as an anti-cancer drug?
blocks.explanation: Cisplatin is used as an anti-cancer drug; transplatin does not show such property (18.9.1).

book_ref.quote: cisplatin is used as an anti-cancer drug, while transplatin does not show such property

blocks.prompt: 122 Transplatin is nonpolar because:

options.text: the bond dipoles of identical ligands point in opposite directions and cancel

blocks.explanation: In transplatin the bond dipoles of identical ligands are opposite and cancel; in cisplatin they do not, so it is polar (18.9.1).

book_ref.quote: making the molecule nonpolar

blocks.prompt: 123 How many geometrical isomers does the [MA₄B₂] type octahedral complex [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]³⁺ have?
blocks.explanation: An [MA₄B₂] octahedral complex has only two geometrical isomers, cis and trans (18.9.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: is an [MA₄B₂] type octahedral complex

blocks.prompt: 124 In trans-[Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]³⁺, the two H₂O ligands are at an angle of:
blocks.explanation: In the trans isomer the two H₂O ligands occupy opposite positions at 180°; in cis they are at 90° (18.9.1).

book_ref.quote: while in the trans isomer, they occupy opposite positions at a 180° angle

blocks.prompt: 125 Inside a cancer cell, cisplatin is 'activated' by a ligand exchange in which:
blocks.explanation: Cisplatin undergoes ligand exchange in which water replaces its chloride ions; it then binds to guanine in DNA (18.9.1).

book_ref.quote: where water replaces its chloride ions

blocks.prompt: 126 The anticancer action of cisplatin was discovered accidentally when:

options.text: platinum electrodes inhibited bacterial cell division

blocks.explanation: Its discovery was accidental, found when platinum electrodes inhibited bacterial cell division (18.9.1).

book_ref.quote: found when platinum electrodes inhibited bacterial cell division

blocks.prompt: 127 Cross-links formed by activated cisplatin in DNA prevent DNA replication and trigger:
blocks.explanation: The structural damage prevents DNA replication, triggering programmed cell death (apoptosis) (18.9.1).

book_ref.quote: triggering programmed cell death (apoptosis)

blocks.prompt: 128 Optical isomers are:

options.text: non-superimposable mirror images of each other

blocks.explanation: Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of each other (18.9.2).

book_ref.quote: Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

blocks.prompt: 129 A pair of non-superimposable mirror-image complexes such as the two forms of [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ is called:
blocks.explanation: Such pairs of molecules are called enantiomers (18.9.2).

book_ref.quote: Such pairs of molecules are called enantiomers.

blocks.prompt: 130 Optical isomerism is commonly shown by:

options.text: square planar complexes with four identical ligands

blocks.explanation: Optical isomerism is commonly shown by octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands, e.g. [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ (18.9.2).

book_ref.quote: commonly shown by octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands

blocks.prompt: 131 The two enantiomers of [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ rotate the plane of polarized light:
blocks.explanation: Optical isomers rotate the plane of polarized light in opposite directions (18.9.2).

book_ref.quote: rotate the plane of polarized light in opposite directions

blocks.prompt: 132 A redox reaction of transition metal ions is feasible when:
blocks.explanation: A reaction is feasible if the overall cell potential E°cell is positive (18.10).

book_ref.quote: A reaction is feasible if the overall cell potential (E°cell) is positive.

blocks.prompt: 133 Of two half-reactions, the species with the more positive E° value:
blocks.explanation: The species with the more positive E° is reduced; the one with the less positive value is oxidized (18.10).

book_ref.quote: the species with the more positive E° value will be reduced

blocks.prompt: 134 E°cell of a redox reaction is calculated as:
blocks.explanation: E°cell = E°reduction − E°oxidation, using reduction potentials of the two half-reactions (18.10).

book_ref.quote: The feasibility of a redox reaction is determined by comparing the standard electrode potentials

blocks.prompt: 135 In the reaction of acidified MnO₄⁻ with C₂O₄²⁻ ions, MnO₄⁻:

options.text: is reduced to Mn²⁺ and acts as the oxidizing agent

blocks.explanation: MnO₄⁻ (E° = +1.52 V) is reduced to Mn²⁺, acting as the oxidizing agent; C₂O₄²⁻ is oxidized to CO₂ (18.10.1).

book_ref.quote: the MnO₄⁻ ion is more likely to be reduced to Mn²⁺ (acting as the oxidizing agent)

blocks.prompt: 136 Taking E°(MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺) = +1.52 V and E°(2CO₂/C₂O₄²⁻) = −0.49 V, E°cell for the oxidation of C₂O₄²⁻ by acidified MnO₄⁻ is:
blocks.explanation: E°cell = 1.52 − (−0.49) = +2.01 V, so the reaction is feasible (18.10.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: The number of electrons lost must be equal to number of electrons gained.

blocks.prompt: 137 In the balanced equation 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O, the total number of electrons transferred is:
blocks.explanation: The reduction half (5e⁻) is multiplied by 2 and the oxidation half (2e⁻) by 5: 10 electrons (18.10.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: It is done by multiplying the two half reactions with different coefficients.

blocks.prompt: 138 How many moles of MnO₄⁻ are needed to oxidize 0.0150 mol of C₂O₄²⁻ ions in acid solution?

book_ref.quote: the C₂O₄²⁻ ion must be oxidized to CO₂ (acting as the reducing agent)

blocks.prompt: 139 Taking E°(MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺) = +1.52 V and E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V, E°cell for the oxidation of Fe²⁺ by acidified MnO₄⁻ is:
blocks.explanation: E°cell = 1.52 − 0.77 = +0.75 V, so the reaction is feasible (18.10.2, book correction).

book_ref.quote: This redox reaction involves the reduction of MnO₄⁻ and the oxidation of Fe²⁺

blocks.prompt: 140 In the balanced equation MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O, one mole of MnO₄⁻ oxidizes:
blocks.explanation: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 electrons and each Fe²⁺ loses 1, so 1 mol MnO₄⁻ oxidizes 5 mol Fe²⁺ (18.10.2).

book_ref.quote: Combine and balance the two equations and sum up their standard electrode potentials

blocks.prompt: 141 20.0 cm³ of 0.120 mol dm⁻³ Fe²⁺ solution is titrated in acid with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. The volume of KMnO₄ needed is:

book_ref.quote: The positive value of the standard electrode potential indicates that this reaction will proceed to the right

blocks.prompt: 142 Excess potassium iodide is added to copper(II) sulphate solution. The products are:

options.text: a white precipitate of CuI and I₂ in solution

blocks.explanation: 2Cu²⁺(aq) + 4I⁻(aq) → 2CuI(s) (white ppt) + I₂(aq) (red-brown solution) (18.10.3).

book_ref.quote: When an excess of potassium iodide is added to an aqueous solution of copper(II) sulphate

blocks.prompt: 143 From E°(Cu²⁺/Cu⁺) = +0.15 V and E°(½I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V, the net standard potential for Cu²⁺ oxidizing I⁻ is:
blocks.explanation: E° = 0.15 − 0.54 = −0.39 V; yet the reaction goes forward because CuI precipitates (18.10.3).

book_ref.quote: the overall reaction proceeds forward despite a calculated negative net standard potential

blocks.prompt: 144 The reaction 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → 2CuI + I₂ goes forward despite a negative net E° because:

options.text: I₂ is a gas and escapes
Cu²⁺ is a stronger reducing agent than I⁻
the reaction is catalysed by water
CuI precipitates, removing Cu⁺ and shifting the equilibrium to the right

blocks.explanation: CuI continuously precipitates, removing Cu⁺ and shifting the equilibrium right (Le Chatelier's principle) (18.10.3).

book_ref.quote: CuI formed is continuously precipitating out of the solution

blocks.prompt: 145 The amount of I₂ formed in the reaction of Cu²⁺ with I⁻ can be found by titration with:
blocks.explanation: The I₂ formed can be quantified by titrating it with a thiosulfate solution (18.10.3).

book_ref.quote: can be quantified by titrating it with a thiosulfate solution

blocks.prompt: 146 Since the Cu²⁺/Cu⁺ couple (+0.15 V) has a lower E° than the I₂/I⁻ couple (+0.54 V), the E° values suggest:

options.text: Cu⁺ is a better reducing agent than I⁻
I⁻ is a better reducing agent than Cu⁺
Cu²⁺ is a better oxidizing agent than I₂

blocks.explanation: The lower E° of Cu²⁺/Cu⁺ suggests Cu⁺ is a better reducing agent than I⁻ (18.10.3).

book_ref.quote: suggesting Cu⁺ is a better reducing agent than I⁻

blocks.prompt: 147 When 0.0100 mol of Cu²⁺ reacts completely with excess I⁻ (2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → 2CuI + I₂), the amount of I₂ formed is:
blocks.explanation: 2 mol Cu²⁺ give 1 mol I₂, so 0.0100 ÷ 2 = 0.00500 mol I₂ (18.10.3).
